title: Pressurization
summary: Read the cabin as a pressure system, recognize a failure early, and preserve useful time for a safe response.
objectives: Distinguish aircraft altitude, cabin altitude, cabin rate, and differential pressure.
Explain how inflow, outflow, and relief functions control cabin pressure.
Recognize both gradual and rapid loss of pressurization.
Apply the additional oxygen rules for pressurized operations without confusing flight level with cabin altitude.

sections.title: One airplane, two altitude environments
sections.body:
Aircraft altitude describes the airplane’s position in the atmosphere. Cabin pressure altitude describes the pressure experienced by its occupants. A pressurized airplane can therefore fly at a high flight level while maintaining a much lower cabin altitude.

Three cabin indications answer different questions: cabin altitude shows the present pressure environment, cabin rate shows how rapidly it is changing, and differential pressure shows the inside-to-outside pressure difference. Compare all three with the AFM/POH schedule and limits. An apparently normal aircraft altimeter does not establish that the cabin is safe, and a low cabin altitude does not by itself prove that structural pressure limits are respected.
sections.deep: Why: Outside pressure falls as the aircraft climbs. To keep cabin altitude low, the system must maintain a larger pressure difference across the structure. Once the aircraft’s allowable differential is reached, the cabin altitude generally must rise with further aircraft climb. Pressurization performance is a compromise between occupant environment, air supply, and the pressure vessel’s limits.

sections.title: Control the air leaving the cabin
sections.body:
A typical system supplies compressed air and meters its escape through an outflow valve. Restricting outflow tends to raise cabin pressure and lower cabin altitude, provided enough air is entering. Increasing outflow tends to reduce cabin pressure. The controller commands the valve according to the selected or programmed cabin schedule.

The safety functions are distinct. Positive-pressure relief protects against excessive inside-to-outside pressure difference. Negative-pressure relief helps prevent outside pressure from exceeding cabin pressure beyond the permitted limit. The installed architecture, air source, controls, and automatic logic vary by airplane. Learn the actual system diagram and limitations rather than transplanting a turbine-aircraft procedure into a pressurized piston airplane.
sections.deep: Why: Pressurization is a mass-flow balance. A commanded closed valve cannot maintain pressure when inflow is lost or leakage becomes too large. Conversely, a stuck or miscommanded valve can produce an abnormal trend even while the air source operates. The diagnosis therefore considers source, control, leakage, and indications together. Use the aircraft’s procedure to determine actions; this explanation is a system model.

sections.title: Monitor the trend before the alarm
sections.body:
Before departure, review the required pressurization configuration, destination elevation, expected cabin schedule, oxygen readiness, and abnormal indications for that airplane. During climb and cruise, compare actual cabin altitude and rate with the expected trend. A slowly increasing cabin altitude at constant aircraft altitude can be an early warning even before occupants feel different.

During descent, cabin pressure must change in a controlled way and reach the appropriate landing condition. Do not improvise a dump or valve sequence from a generic description. Remaining differential pressure on the ground, an unusual cabin rate, or a warning must be handled according to the AFM/POH.
sections.deep: Apply it: The airplane remains level at its cruise flight level, but cabin altitude climbs steadily and differential pressure falls. The aircraft’s height is unchanged; the occupants’ environment is deteriorating. Recognizing that combination early preserves the ability to use oxygen and respond deliberately. Waiting for euphoria, headache, or a dramatic pressure event wastes the warning provided by the instruments.

sections.title: Gradual and rapid failures need early recognition
sections.body:
A gradual failure may have little noise or physical sensation. Its danger is that the cabin altitude can increase while the pilot’s judgment deteriorates. A rapid decompression may produce a loud event, cooling, fog, airflow, and sudden physiological exposure. The severity depends on aircraft altitude, cabin volume, opening size, and other conditions.

Preserve breathing and aircraft control immediately, then execute the aircraft-specific emergency procedure. That generally includes prompt use of appropriate oxygen and an emergency descent when required, coordinated with terrain, traffic, and structural or speed limitations. Treat the aircraft checklist and training as the authority for configuration and sequence.
sections.deep: Why: Useful decision time shrinks sharply at high cabin altitudes, and rapid decompression can reduce it further. An oxygen mask buried in a bag is not functionally ready. Practice locating and operating the actual equipment while on the ground. Brief passengers and assign crew tasks before flight so that recognition does not have to be followed by an improvised discussion.

sections.title: Additional oxygen protection at high flight levels
sections.body:
For a pressurized aircraft, §91.211(b) adds requirements based on aircraft flight altitude. Above FL250, provide each occupant at least a ten-minute emergency oxygen supply in addition to oxygen otherwise required by the general cabin-altitude rule.

Above FL350, the ordinary rule requires a pilot at the controls to wear and use the specified oxygen mask. The two-pilot quick-donning exception applies at or below FL410 when both pilots are at the controls and each has a qualifying mask that can be donned with one hand within five seconds, secured, sealed, and delivering oxygen. Above FL350, if one pilot leaves the controls, the remaining pilot must use a mask until the other returns.
sections.deep: Apply it: A normal low cabin altitude does not remove the emergency-supply requirement above FL250. The high-flight-level rule prepares for the cabin that could exist after a failure, while the general rule addresses the current cabin environment. These are layered protections. Do not substitute the older FL450 exception sometimes shown in notes for the current FL410 text.

sections.title: Qualification follows aircraft capability
sections.body:
Section 61.31(g) establishes additional training and endorsement requirements for acting as PIC of the defined high-altitude pressurized aircraft. Its capability test uses the lower of service ceiling and maximum operating altitude: that value must be above 25,000 feet MSL. Do not decide applicability solely from today’s planned cruise altitude.

The ordinary pathway includes documented ground training in physiology, high-altitude conditions, decompression, and related subjects, plus flight training and a proficiency endorsement. The flight portion covers high-altitude cruise, a simulated rapid-decompression response without actually depressurizing the aircraft, and emergency descent procedures. Review the rule’s documented exceptions before concluding that new training is required.
sections.deep: Apply it: Planning to fly a qualifying airplane only at 18,000 feet does not itself remove the qualification requirement. The aircraft-capability rule and the oxygen operating rule answer different questions. This lesson supplies conceptual preparation; it does not issue an endorsement or replace the required aircraft or approved-device training and instructor determination.

sections.title: Why decompression changes more than oxygen
sections.body:
At a given temperature, a trapped gas tends to expand as surrounding pressure falls. A decompression can therefore affect ears, sinuses, and other gas spaces while simultaneously reducing oxygen availability. Cabin temperature may drop, and visible condensation can appear as the air expands and cools. Neither fog nor its absence alone describes the full severity of the event.

The pressure vessel also carries mechanical load. For a simplified panel, force equals differential pressure multiplied by area. A modest pressure difference across a large area creates a substantial force, which is why relief functions and operating limitations matter. Actual fuselage stresses and door behavior depend on structure and design.
sections.deep: Deeper connection: Boyle’s-law reasoning, pV approximately constant for a fixed gas amount at constant temperature, helps explain trapped-gas expansion. It is a teaching approximation for a gas pocket, not a complete transient model of a leaking, cooling cabin. Use it to explain the direction of change while relying on the aircraft design and AFM/POH for actual limitations and responses.

teachBack: Explain a rising cabin altitude and falling differential while aircraft altitude stays constant.
Draw the inflow, outflow valve, cabin, and relief functions for the airplane being taught.
Explain which oxygen rules use cabin pressure altitude and which use aircraft flight level.
takeaways: Aircraft altitude and cabin altitude are different measurements.
The outflow controller regulates pressure, but it depends on adequate inflow and acceptable leakage.
Slow pressure loss can incapacitate without a dramatic decompression event.
The current two-pilot quick-donning exception uses FL410, with specific conditions.

quiz.question: At constant aircraft altitude, cabin altitude rises while differential pressure falls. What does that combination suggest?
options: The cabin is becoming more highly pressurized.
The airplane must be climbing.
The cabin pressure environment is deteriorating despite level aircraft flight.
The aircraft altimeter proves the cabin is safe.
feedback: Rising cabin altitude corresponds to lower cabin pressure, not greater pressurization.
The scenario explicitly holds aircraft altitude constant.
The cabin can lose pressure independently of the airplane’s flight altitude.
The aircraft altimeter does not measure the occupant pressure environment.

quiz.question: In a simplified functioning system with adequate inflow, what tends to happen when the outflow valve restricts escaping air?
options: Cabin pressure rises and cabin altitude falls.
Cabin pressure always becomes equal to outside pressure.
The airplane’s flight altitude automatically decreases.
The oxygen percentage becomes 100 percent.
feedback: Retaining more of the supplied air tends to raise cabin pressure.
Equalization generally results from releasing pressure or losing the ability to retain it.
The valve controls the cabin environment rather than aircraft flight path.
Pressurizing ordinary air does not make it pure oxygen.
quiz.hint: Trace the balance between air entering and leaving.

quiz.question: Why is gradual pressurization loss especially insidious?
options: It always produces a loud bang first.
The pilot can lose judgment before recognizing an obvious event.
It cannot raise cabin altitude.
It eliminates the need for oxygen equipment.
feedback: A slow failure may have few dramatic physical cues.
A gradual rise in cabin altitude can impair the person expected to diagnose it.
Loss of cabin pressure corresponds to rising cabin pressure altitude.
Pressurization loss is one reason emergency oxygen readiness matters.
quiz.hint: Consider who must recognize the failure and how hypoxia affects that person.

quiz.question: A pressurized airplane has a normal cabin altitude while cruising above FL250. What extra protection does the general Part 91 rule require?
options: No oxygen because the cabin is normal.
Only a pulse oximeter for each occupant.
An unlimited oxygen supply for every occupant.
At least a ten-minute emergency oxygen supply for every occupant, additional to other required oxygen.
feedback: The emergency supply addresses a future loss of pressurization.
A monitoring device does not replace the required oxygen supply.
The provision specifies a minimum emergency supply rather than unlimited endurance.
The rule adds an emergency reserve even when the current cabin environment is normal.
quiz.hint: The high-flight-level rule anticipates a cabin failure.

quiz.question: At FL390, two pilots are at the controls with qualifying quick-donning masks available. One pilot leaves the controls. Under §91.211(b), what must the remaining pilot do?
options: Continue relying solely on the two-pilot exception.
Wait until the cabin reaches 15,000 feet.
Put on and use the oxygen mask until the other pilot returns.
Descend below FL450 before considering oxygen.
feedback: The exception’s two-pilots-at-the-controls condition is no longer satisfied.
The remaining-pilot requirement is triggered by the flight-level and crew-location condition.
Above FL350, the remaining pilot must use a mask while the other is away.
FL450 is not the applicable current quick-donning exception threshold.
quiz.hint: Check the requirement that applies when one pilot leaves.

quiz.question: A simplified cabin panel has an area of 100 square inches and a differential pressure of 5 pounds per square inch. What is the resulting force magnitude?
options: 20 pounds-force.
500 pounds-force.
105 pounds-force.
5 pounds-force.
feedback: Dividing area by pressure does not give force.
Force equals pressure difference times area: 5 times 100 equals 500 pounds-force.
Adding area and pressure is dimensionally invalid.
The pressure must act across the full panel area.
quiz.hint: Multiply pressure difference by area and check units.
